issue_context.title: Remove "relationship" stutter in relationship attribute macro
issue_context.body:
## What problem does this solve or what need does it fill?

Current

```rust 
#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship(relationship_target = TargetedBy)]
struct Targeting(Entity);

#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship_target(relationship = Targeting)]
struct TargetedBy(Vec<Entity>);
```

Proposed

```rust 
#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship(target = TargetedBy)]
struct Targeting(Entity);

#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[target(relationship = Targeting)]
struct TargetedBy(Vec<Entity>);
```

I think the proposed syntax is more readable than what we have now.
comments:
`#[target]` seems ambiguous to me. How about these?

```rust
#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship(target = TargetedBy)]
struct Targeting(Entity);

#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship_target(source = Targeting)]
struct TargetedBy(Vec<Entity>);
```

```rust
#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship(target = TargetedBy)]
struct Targeting(Entity);

#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship(source = Targeting)]
struct TargetedBy(Vec<Entity>);
```

Thanks for the suggestion - I like that it's explicit about `Targeting` being the source of truth for the relationship. Personally your second suggestion is my favorite of the three so far - would be curious to hear others opinions.

My preference goes to either the currently implemented syntax in my PR, or the second suggestion by @nxsaken.

Let me know if I should change it!

If Relationships in bevy will always contain bi-directionality:

I like both the current and originally proposed suggestions because `relationship(target = x)` + `target(relationship =x )`  has a symmetry between the tokens used to express the directionality of the relationship, which makes it consistent.

Renaming the tokens isn't important, but breaking the symmetry would be a bad idea.

If Relationships in Bevy will not always be directional, or not always bi-directional:

I like @nxsaken's second suggestion, as it would be much easier to expand this form to represent non-directional or uni-directional relationships.

Another +1 in favor of @nxsaken's second suggestion. Here's one more possibility:

```rust
#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship_source(target = TargetedBy)]
struct Targeting(Entity);

#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[relationship_target(source = Targeting)]
struct TargetedBy(Vec<Entity>);
```

Which is basically the same thing, but a little more verbose.
I think it is safe to say @nxsaken's second suggestion is the most popular so far, so I will update the PR to implement that.

review_comments:
I think that the top-level attributes should correspond _directly_ to the name of the traits being defined. As written, there is literally no indicator that this Component is a RelationshipTarget. No amount of saved text is worth that level of implicitness / context-erasure. Not including an explicit RelationshipTarget derive is already a level of jank that is pushing the boundaries.

I'm _more_ open to the `source` / `target` names to avoid stutter, but from my perspective the stutter _makes sense_. We have exactly two trait names here: `Relationship` and `RelationshipTarget`. The `relationship` attribute produces a `Relationship` trait impl. The `relationship_target` attribute produces a `RelationshipTarget` trait impl. Likewise, when these traits connect to each other, they use the `Relationship::RelationshipTarget` and `RelationshipTarget::Relationship` associated types. The 1:1 mapping here was intentional. By using `source` and `target`, we are introducing new concept names. Developers need to learn that arbitrarily `source` == `RelationshipTarget::Relationship` and `target` == `Relationship::RelationshipTarget`. I do not think this is helpful for people.

I personally think we should keep the attributes as-is, as they are the most direct maps to the types and terms that we actually use.

I agree that it's preferable to have attributes map to the traits they implement.

However, I also see macro attributes as a pseudo dsl that can help in understanding what's going on from a quick glance. From that perspective the current naming unfortunately feels like word soup (it certainly doesn't help that relationship is a long word).

```rust
#[relationship(relationship_target = ...)]
#[relationship_target(relationship = ...)]
```

It's difficult for me to parse what's going on at a glance - even knowing what I'm supposed to be looking at beforehand.

Personally it was a little jarring for me that `Relationship` is one end of the relationship, and `RelationshipTarget` is the other. Intuitively I felt like a `Relationship` should describe the edge between two entities. It took reading the docs, and mentally putting together that `Relationship` is the "source of truth" for it to click for me. In this case I think introducing the `source` keyword/concept could be a good thing for DX.

If we do something like

```rust
#[relationship_source(target = ...)]
#[relationship_target(source = ...)]
```

and don't mind renaming `Relationship` -> `RelationshipSource` we could have attributes matching trait names and easier to read attribute macros.

This one is similar to JPA annotations:

```rust
#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[many_to_one(inverse = Children)] // Relationship -> ManyToOne, owning side
struct ChildOf(Entity);

#[derive(Component, Debug)]
#[one_to_many(owned_by = ChildOf)] // RelationshipTarget -> OneToMany, inverse side
struct Children(Vec<Entity>);
```

Giving the "nice" Relationship name to the "relationship source" was intentional. The feature is "relationships" and the behavior-driving type is the Relationship type. I think having an actual type we can point to that "is" a Relationship is a useful simplifying concept. A Relationship is a one-directional edge. A RelationshipTarget is the collection of all reverse edges for a given relationship. To me, asking "what is this RelationshipTarget's Relationship?" is no more confusing than asking "What is this RelationshipTarget's  RelationshipSource?". The addition of the "source" context in some ways confuses things more, as it creates the question "where is the relationship?" With the current terminology, someone can ask "what is the relationship?" and the answer is easily ChildOf.

I'm still of the opinion that we should try very hard to treat concept names as actual symbols. It is true that we are building DSLs here, but from my perspective it should be the most rust-ey, statically-typed DSL it can be. One way to do that is to treat concept names and attributes as actual symbols.

I personally find the `A->B` and `B->A` symbol relationship helpful in creating a true binding between the two types.

```rust
#[derive(Component)]
#[relationship(relationship_target = Children)]
struct ChildOf(Entity);

#[derive(Component)]
#[relationship_target(relationship = ChildOf)]
struct Children(Vec<Entity>);
```

This makes a number of things clear:

1. `ChildOf` _is_ the Relationship. That is a very strong hint that if I want to add a relationship, I should use that component. 
2. These are the reverse of each other, thanks to the full `A->B`, `B->A` symbol parity.
3. I know that ChildOf's `relationship_target` is Children. When I see the `RelationshipTarget` trait somewhere in code, I can trivially make the connection because the terms are identical.
4. I know that Children's `relationship` is `ChildOf`. When I see the `Relationship` trait somewhere in code, I can trivially make the connection because the terms are identical.

From my perspective, the current names and symbols are already optimal.

That makes sense - I can see how that maps better to the underlying implementation. I'll maintain that it can be confusing when you first start working with it - at the end of the day it's a trade off between that initial weirdness, and being faithful to not hiding what's happening under the hood.

No intent to pointlessly bike-shed so I'll defer to your judgement.
